as_read: Mixed: modest pooled capsaicin weight effect, a null single-dose trial at the labels' 500 mg, and small positive gut trials at other doses or coatings; labels print no capsaicinoid amount.

studies_to_add.primary_endpoint: not named; thermogenesis and fat oxidation
studies_to_add.quote: These results suggest that acute ingestion of 500 mg of cayenne (1.25 mg capsaicin) or evodiamine is not effective at inducing thermogenesis and increasing fat oxidation at rest or during exercise in men.
The current meta-analysis suggests that capsaicin supplementation may have rather modest effects in reducing BMI, BW and WC for overweight or obese individuals.
Red pepper was more effective than placebo in decreasing the intensity of dyspeptic symptoms, probably through a desensitization of gastric nociceptive C-fibres induced by its content of capsaicin.

stop_list: Heat units on labels (40,000 SHU or STU) can't be expressed as a capsaicinoid dose and aren't converted
No capsaicinoid declaration on any of the 26 labels, per the label rows read
clinician_items: 21573941: in the IBS trial, 6 red pepper patients dropped out for abdominal pain against 2 placebo dropouts, and 8 patients had pills reduced because of abdominal pain at the start.
33291700: a single 2 g chili capsule dose in non-erosive reflux patients gave more severe abdominal burning (p<0.05) and a trend to more severe heartburn (p=0.06) than placebo.
stored_rating_note: The stored material_form says standardized extract or powder, but the labels print no standard. The stored sample size of 191 is the meta-analysis's pooled number, for a single-meal energy intake outcome. The stored record cites no trial at the labels' cayenne amount.
